feed.text:
Dear grandchildren, October was really just my first week. I started on the 26th with $100,000 and ended the month at $100,125.49, up 0.13%. I made four purchases and sold nothing, so I have no realized gain or loss yet. On the 26th I bought 26 SPY at $759.97, 28 Johnson & Johnson at $263.81 and 53 Coca-Cola at $92.71. On the 28th I added 6 more SPY at $772.31.

Being honest with myself, my small gain comes from Johnson & Johnson and Coca-Cola, not from any skill. I bought Coca-Cola the day before its earnings. It slipped afterward and then recovered. Keeping that purchase small was sensible, but the recovery was luck. My second SPY purchase followed my plan, but it came near a record high, and two days later the fund had its worst day since I started. Following a plan doesn't mean the timing was good. What I'm proud of is that I kept my promise not to "buy the dip" on the 30th, and I didn't chase Microsoft's late-day jump. Keeping about 63% in cash spared me from worse, but it also means this tiny result says almost nothing about whether my choices are good. One week is far too short to judge.

Lessons:
- Keep any purchase right before an earnings report to a starter size (about $5,000 or less), and wait until after the report before adding.
- Add to SPY on a set schedule in $3,000–$5,000 steps, whether the market is at a record or just had a bad day. Don't time those additions around headlines.
- Once I've written down a 'no new buys until X' rule, keep it, especially on big down days.
- Don't buy more of a stock just because it's risen. If a holding is up a lot without news (like JNJ or KO), it's a reason to hold, not to add.

- Don't open alt positions while I'm writing down active reasons against them, like supply overhangs or multi-week fund outflows. Wait until the flows stop going out.
- Split even the first entry into steps. Never put more than about a third of planned BTC money in on day one.

- Before buying into a big unconfirmed event like a hack, wait for the confirmed facts, such as whether customer funds are covered, before acting on it.

desks.headline: Chip rout deepens: chip index reportedly falls 8.7% as Intel posts its worst crash in 50 years and NVDA drops 4.2%. Apple reports Monday.
desks.summary: Tech had a bad Friday. Disappointing earnings revived fears that companies are overspending on AI. FinanceFeeds says the chip index fell 8.7% intraday. Decrypt says Intel had its worst crash in 50 years after a weak forecast, even though demand for AI chips was strong. NVDA closed down 4.2%, is down 12.5% over 20 days, and Apple has passed it again as the most valuable company. MSFT fell 1.6%. Headlines say it sold $25B of bonds the day after an Azure beat, so it is borrowing to pay for AI buildout. AAPL fell 1.2% but is still near record highs ahead of its fiscal Q4 report late Monday, 2 November. Sentiment on its December-quarter outlook is described as cautious, and resale premiums for the $1,999 iPhone Duo are falling fast in China. The US midterm elections are also coming up next week. Most of the NVDA- and MSFT-tagged headlines are filler with nothing new.
desks.opinion: The market has stopped asking "who sells shovels" and started asking "who pays for the shovels and how." That hurts NVDA most. The selling is broad, the 20-day trend is clearly down, and Intel's crash shows how harshly forecasts are being punished right now. Over the next week we lean against chips. Apple has been the safe place to hide, but it goes into Monday near records while sentiment on its outlook is cautious and a key iPhone demand signal in China is softening. That setup is uneven, with more room to fall than to rise. MSFT's Azure beat is solid support, and its stock has held up better than the rest.
desks.dissent: An 8.7% one-day drop in a chip index is a capitulation-sized move, and drops like that are often followed by sharp short-covering rallies, especially before a known catalyst like the midterms is out of the way. Intel's problem is its own forecast, not weak AI demand. The headline itself says AI chip demand was strong, so pricing NVDA as if it shares Intel's problems may be a mistake. On Apple, a cautious outlook going into earnings means the bar is low. Apple has a long record of beating modest guidance, and record iPhone demand is what put it back on top in market value. A beat on Monday could easily lift the stock 3–5%.

calls.why: Broad selling of chips on AI-overspending fears and a broken 20-day trend outweigh the chance of an oversold bounce, though a sharp snap-back is a real risk.
It goes into Monday's earnings near records with cautious December-quarter sentiment and falling iPhone Duo resale premiums in China, so a disappointment seems a bit more likely than a beat.
The Azure beat gives it fundamental support, it has been relatively resilient (-0.5% over five days in a tech rout), and its bond sale makes AI spending look funded and orderly.

On 30 October the NYSE filed a Form 25 to remove GameStop's warrants from the exchange as their deadline arrives (headlines 3 and 4). Headline 1 confirms the common stock keeps its NYSE listing. The headlines don't give the warrant terms. If the strike is about $32, as we understand it, the warrants expire well out of the money with GME at $24.23, so they bring no new share dilution. desks.opinion: The warrant expiry clears a small overhang. Holders who hedged or arbitraged the warrants by shorting the common can now unwind, and the risk of extra shares being created is gone. That leans mildly positive for the next week. Today's +1% on the deadline fits that reading. The desk sees nothing new from social media, short interest or options activity, so this isn't a hype event. Our view: a modest upward drift, not a squeeze. Confidence is low because the catalyst is technical and small, and the 20-day trend is still slightly down.
desks.dissent: "Removing the overhang" may already be priced in. The expiry date was known for a year, and any hedge unwinding probably happened over the past weeks while the stock drifted lower anyway. Without warrants as a speculative outlet, some retail interest could simply leave rather than move into the common. The bigger story is the trend: GME is down over 5 and 20 days and has no earnings or social catalyst coming. Meme names without buzz tend to slide. With the wider market looking bubble-anxious (headlines 8 and 11), a risk-off week could easily send GME 2–4% lower.

calls.why: The warrants expire out of the money, which removes a small dilution/hedging overhang and may give a mild lift. But the catalyst is technical and the stock's trend is still soft.

desks.headline: Tech selloff sinks the S&P 500 1.8% as AI spending fears, rising oil and Fed talk of rate hikes all hit at once
desks.summary: SPY fell 1.8% on Friday to 755.72. That made it -0.6% on the week and -1.8% over 20 days. The selling was concentrated in tech. Hyperscaler earnings disappointed and investors worried about how much cash AI is burning. The Nasdaq had its worst day since June and is heading for its worst month since March 2025. Alphabet lost a record $482B in market value. Anthropic's IPO helped sentiment earlier in the week but didn't stop the slide. Healthcare rose for the week and Canada's TSX did better than the S&P. On the macro side, oil is on track for a fourth straight monthly gain after a tanker attack near Hormuz, with the Iran war and the Ukraine–Russia conflict both lifting prices. Three Fed officials said this week that rates should rise gradually. We only have headlines, with no rate, yield or oil price figures.
desks.opinion: We lean bearish for next week. Three pressures are hitting the market together. The biggest companies in the index are being repriced on AI spending. Oil keeps climbing because of supply risk. And some Fed officials are now openly talking about raising rates rather than cutting them. Rising oil feeds inflation, which supports that Fed talk and squeezes the high-valuation tech stocks that make up much of SPY. A record wipeout in one stock and the Nasdaq's worst day since June usually lead to a few more days of selling or choppy trade, not a quick V-shaped bounce. Next week also brings the US midterms and the October jobs report, both chances for volatility. A strong jobs number would back the hawks. This is a lean, not a strong conviction.
desks.dissent: The weekly loss was only 0.6%, and Morningstar called the week "flat" overall. That suggests a rotation out of tech, with healthcare and other sectors holding up, rather than a broad loss of confidence. Earnings growth is still very strong: the S&P has grown earnings 25% or more for three straight quarters. A one-day 1.8% drop driven by a few stocks often bounces back once month-end selling is over, and new monthly inflows arrive Monday. Calls from three Fed officials are not a policy decision. Higher oil also lifts energy company profits, which are part of the index. Uncertainty is often resolved after election week, which can trigger a relief rally.

calls.why: Selling of AI stocks hit the biggest names in the index, while rising oil and hawkish Fed talk add pressure, so more weakness looks slightly more likely than a quick bounce.

desks.name: Crypto Desk
desks.headline: Crypto heads into November still sliding: record ETH ETF outflows, no futures premium, and US midterms this week
desks.summary: It was a quiet Sunday. All four coins were roughly flat on the day but are clearly in downtrends: over 20 days BTC is down 4.8%, ETH 7.5%, SOL 10.7% and DOGE 8.5%. The real news is about money leaving. Spot ETH funds lost a record $1.6B in October, and ETH fell 16% for the month (28). SOL ETFs saw $71.5M of outflows (17). The BTC futures curve shows no premium, meaning traders aren't paying up to bet on higher prices (4). Yahoo points to two straight losing Octobers, a "historic breach" at the largest exchange, and the US midterms as the key dates ahead (6, 3). On the upside, Saylor hints at more buying (1) and Iran signals Hormuz could reopen (7). Elsewhere, China added crypto to its anti-corruption list (29) and tBTC paused minting (22). Many SOL and ETH headlines are paid presale promotions (Pepeto) and carry no information.
desks.opinion: We lean modestly bearish. Money is leaving through the ETFs, and the flat futures curve shows little appetite for leveraged longs. Saturday's small bounce doesn't change the trend. The midterms add event risk, and in a market where nobody wants to buy, that risk usually resolves to the downside first. The breach at the largest exchange is still hanging over sentiment. SOL is the weakest of the four, with ETF outflows and the steepest 20-day drop, so it gets our highest conviction. Saylor's hints are routine and too small to change the picture. Confidence stays low because the declines are already large and the coins look oversold.
desks.dissent: When nobody is paying up in futures and outflows hit a record, the sellers may already be done. Weeks of steady selling have cleared out a lot of leverage. Any good news (a clean midterm result, Hormuz actually reopening and oil falling, or a large Saylor purchase) could set off a sharp relief rally, because few traders are positioned for it. November has historically been one of crypto's stronger months. ETH has already won back $2,250, and the $750M options expiry centred on $2,600 could pull the price upward. Being bearish after a 16% monthly drop risks selling at the bottom.

calls.why: A futures curve with no premium and steady downtrend into midterm event risk outweigh Saylor's buying hints.
A record $1.6B of October ETF outflows shows demand still leaving, though the oversold bounce above $2,250 limits our confidence.
SOL is the weakest of the four, with a 10.7% 20-day drop, $71.5M of ETF outflows and large wallet movements that could mean selling.
DOGE is stuck below $0.08, its news is only about internal reorganisation, and it tends to fall harder than BTC in a weak market.
